instruction: Can you explain Doctor Of Medicine?
output: Postgraduate medical degree This article is about the professional degree. For the person or occupation (medical doctor), see Physician . M.D. diploma conferred on James Maxwell Ferguson by the University of Edinburgh in 1841 A Doctor of Medicine (abbreviated M.D. or MD , from the Latin Medicinae Doctor or Dr med. , from the inverse construction) is a medical degree , the meaning of which varies between different jurisdictions. In the United States , and some other countries, the MD denotes a professional degree of physician . This generally arose because many in 18th-century medical professions trained in Scotland , which used the MD degree nomenclature. [ 1 ] In England, however, Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) was used: in the 19th century, it became the standard in Scotland too. Thus, in the United Kingdom , Ireland and other countries, the MD is a research doctorate , honorary doctorate or applied clinical degree restricted to those who already hold a professional degree (Bachelor's/Master's/Doctoral) in medicine. In those countries, the equivalent professional degree to the North American, and some others' usage of MD is still typically titled Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery. [ 2 ] History [ edit ] The thesis presented by Claude Bernard to obtain his doctorate of medicine (1843) The first medical degrees were awarded by the Schola Medica Salernitana around the year 1000, including to women such as Trota of Salerno . [ 3 ] [ 4 ] The degrees received legal sanction in 1137 by Roger II of Sicily and in 1231 by Emperor Federico II , in the Constitution of Melfi . [ 5 ] In the titles XLIV-LXXXIX of the third book of the Constitutions of 1231, it was established that the activity of a physician ( medicus ) could only be carried out by physicians holding a medical degree, the Licentia Medendi (license to medicine), by the Schola Medica Salernitana (the only school in the kingdom authorized to award degrees in medicine). [ 3 ] [ 6 ] This degree was awarded after a curriculum composed of three years of study of logic , five years of medical studies , an examination of a commission composed of the professors of the university, a one-year apprenticeship with an expert doctor, and a final examination before the commissioners of the Royal Curia and the Provincial Curias. [ 6 ] In 1703, the University of Glasgow 's first medical graduate, Samuel Benion, was issued with the academic degree of Doctor of Medicine. [ 7 ] University medical education in England culminated with the MB qualification, and in Scotland the MD, until in the mid-19th century the public bodies who regulated medical practice at the time required practitioners in Scotland as well as England to hold the dual Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery degrees ( MB BS/MBChB/MB BChir/BM BCh etc. ). North American medical schools switched to the tradition of the ancient universities of Scotland and began granting the MD title rather than the MB beginning in the late 18th century. [ 8 ] The Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons in New York (which at the time was referred to as King's College of Medicine) was the first American university to grant the MD degree instead of the MB. [ 9 ] Early medical schools in North America that granted the Doctor of Medicine degrees were Columbia , Penn , Harvard , Maryland , and McGill . [ 10 ] These first few North American medical schools that were established were (for the most part) founded by physicians and surgeons who had been trained in England and Scotland. [ 11 ] [ 1 ] In most countries having a Doctor of Medicine degree does not mean that the individual will be allowed to practice medicine. Typically a physician must go through a year of general medical education in a hospital as an intern and then a residency for at least three years in a specific field of medicine and then take some form of licensing examination in their jurisdiction. Medical occupational licensing was found to increase the time required to allow practicing medicine and increase medical education costs. [ 12 ] A feminine form, "Doctress of Medicine" or Medicinae Doctrix , was also used by the New England Female Medical College in Boston in the 1860s. [ 13 ] [ 14 ] [ 15 ] By country [ edit ] First professional degrees [ edit ] Afghanistan [ edit ] This section does not cite any sources . Please help improve this section by adding citations to reliable sources . Unsourced material may be challenged and removed . ( May 2025 ) ( Learn how and when to remove this message ) In Afghanistan , medical education begins after high school. No pre-medicine courses or bachelor's degree are required. Eligibility is determined through the rank applicants obtain in the public university entrance exam held every year throughout the country. Entry to medical school is competitive, and only students with the highest ranks are accepted into medical programs. The primary medical degree is completed in 7 years. According to the new medical curriculum (from 2016), during the 12th semester, medical students must complete research on a medical topic and provide a thesis as part of their training. Students also undergo a one-year compulsory internship, to be completed in a teaching hospital. Medical graduates are awarded a certificate in general medicine, regarded as "MD" and validated by the "Ministry of Higher Education of Afghanistan". All physicians are to obtain licensing and a medical council registration number from the "Ministry of Public Health" before they officially begin to practice. They may subsequently specialize in a specific medical field at medical schools offering the necessary qualifications. After graduation, students may complete residency . Before the civil wars in Afghanistan, medical education used to be taught by foreign professors or Afghan professors who studied medical education abroad. The Kabul medical institute certified the students as "Master of Medicine". After the civil wars, medical education changed extensively, and the MD certification has been reduced to "Medicine Bachelor". Argentina [ edit ] In Argentina , the First Degree of Physician or Physician Diplomate ( Spanish : Título de Médico ) [ 16 ] is equivalent to the North American MD Degree with six years of intensive studies followed by usually three or four years of residency as a major specialty in a particular empiric field, consisting of internships, social services and sporadic research. Only by holding a Medical Title can the postgraduate student apply for the Doctor degree through a doctorate in medicine program approved by the National Commission for University Evaluation and Accreditation [ es ] . [ 16 ] Armenia [ edit ] In Armenia , medical studies take six years. After completing high school, students can apply to one of the country's medical universities. The application process includes an admission examination testing the applicant in biology, chemistry, and physics. The six-year medical education course is a combined bachelor's and master's degree program. The first three years consist of lecture courses while the final three years consist of education in clinical settings alongside attending physicians. Medical students may also simultaneously study for a Master of Public Health if they wish, which takes one and a half years of study. After the six-year period of study, students must pass the state medical examination to graduate. They must then undergo a period of residency training in their chosen field of practice, the duration of which lasts from one to four years. [ 17 ] Australia [ edit ] See also: Medical education in Australia Historically, Australian medical schools have followed the British tradition by conferring the degrees of Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) to its graduates whilst reserving the title of Doctor of Medicine (MD) for their research training degree, analogous to the PhD , or for their higher or honorary doctorates . Although the majority of Australian MBBS degrees have been graduate programs since the 1990s, under the previous Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) they remained categorized as Level 7 Bachelor's degrees together with other undergraduate programs. The latest version of the AQF includes the new category of Level 9 Master's (Extended) degrees which permits the use of the term 'Doctor' in the styling of the degree title of relevant professional programs. As a result, various Australian medical schools have replaced their MBBS degrees with the MD to resolve the previous anomalous nomenclature. With the introduction of the Master's level MD, universities have also renamed their previous medical research doctorates. The University of Melbourne was the first to introduce the MD in 2011 as a basic medical degree, and has renamed its research degree to Doctor of Medical Science (DMedSc). [ 18 ] Australian National University offers a Doctor of Medicine and Surgery (MChD, abbreviated from Medicinae ac Chirurgiae Doctoranda) which is also a 4-year extended master's degree that qualifies graduates to be medical practitioners like with a MD or MBBS. [ 19 ] Austria [ edit ] In Austria , medical studies (medicine or dentistry) take six years full-time. In medicine, the first two years comprise basic fields of medicine such as anatomy, biology, chemistry, physics, physiology, etc., the next three years consist of all medical fields in the narrower sense with frequent bedside training and medical traineeships while the sixth and last year is dedicated solely to working in a clinic. After this, a specific six-year training (e.g. in internal medicine, paediatrics, ENT, pathology) or four year ( GP ) can be started; without this training, working with patients is forbidden. There is no central placement test for said specialist training, only a board-registered spot as a resident/registrar is needed. As with all other studies in Austria, there is no tuition but compulsory students' union fee (approx €38 per year). A specific entrance exam (MedAT, Medizin-Aufnahmetest, medicine acceptance test) has to be taken but is open only once a year in summer; a fee of €110 has to be paid. In 2019, 16443 persons registered for the MedAT and 12960 took the test. [ 20 ] 1.680 university places for both medicine and dentistry are offered each year with 95% of all places for EU citizens and 75% for applicants with an Austrian higher education entrance qualification/GCE A-levels. Many Germans who are denied studying in their home country try to study medicine in Austria; hence this quota was introduced and approved by the EU as most of them leave upon graduation. [ 21 ] The title of "Doktor" is granted to physicians (Dr. med. univ., Doctor medicinae universae, Dr. der gesamten Heilkunde = Dr. "of the entire art of healing") and dentists (Dr. med. dent., Doctor medicinae dentinae), who do not possess doctorates, but Master's level 6 year-training, similar to the American MD or DDS . [ 22 ] although they have to write a diploma thesis of approx. 50–100 pages. In former days the same title was connected to an official doctoral degree in connection with an older study regulation. [ 23 ] [ circular reference ] [ 24 ] [ 25 ] The law has been changed in 2002. Some of which are published in peer-reviewed journals while others are not. A post-graduate research doctorate (Dr. scient. med., Dr. scientiae medicinae, or PhD ) can be obtained after a three years post-graduate study at a medical university. All doctors may be addressed as "Doktor ______", and the title is usually contracted to "Dr. ______". In many everyday-day settings in Austria, also outside the clinic, it is common to address medical doctors solely as "Herr/Frau Doktor" (Mr./Ms./Mrs. doctor) without any specific family name (especially in rural areas and small villages, and by older people), and they are often viewed as the "real doctors". Among themselves, MDs do not use "doctor" as an appellation but just "Herr Kollege/Frau Kollegin" (Mr./Ms/Mrs. = "dear" colleague). Consistent use of "Doktor" when addressing another medical doctor is seen as confrontative and mockery. Azerbaijan [ edit ] In Azerbaijan , medical education is provided at the "baza ali" (basic higher) level in specialties such as Tibb (Medicine). [ 26 ] Medical programs typically last six years, combining theoretical instruction and clinical training. [ 27 ] After graduation, doctors may continue their training through rezidentura (residency), which lasts between 2–5 years depending on the specialty. [ 28 ] Following residency, physicians receive the professional qualification of "həkim‑mütəxəssis". Some medical specialties also require certification ("sertifikasiya") in order to practice. [ 29 ] Azerbaijani medical degrees are recognized internationally, depending on the country and licensing body. [ 30 ] Belgium [ edit ] This section does not cite any sources . Please help improve this section by adding citations to reliable sources . Unsourced material may be challenged and removed . Physicians would then either have to do a three-year internship to become a general practitioner or up to 6 years to specialize. instruction: What is Doctor Of Medicine?
output: Postgraduate medical degree This article is about the professional degree. For the person or occupation (medical doctor), see Physician . M.D. diploma conferred on James Maxwell Ferguson by the University of Edinburgh in 1841 A Doctor of Medicine (abbreviated M.D. or MD , from the Latin Medicinae Doctor or Dr med. , from the inverse construction) is a medical degree , the meaning of which varies between different jurisdictions. In the United States , and some other countries, the MD denotes a professional degree of physician . This generally arose because many in 18th-century medical professions trained in Scotland , which used the MD degree nomenclature. [ 1 ] In England, however, Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) was used: in the 19th century, it became the standard in Scotland too. Thus, in the United Kingdom , Ireland and other countries, the MD is a research doctorate , honorary doctorate or applied clinical degree restricted to those who already hold a professional degree (Bachelor's/Master's/Doctoral) in medicine. In those countries, the equivalent professional degree to the North American, and some others' usage of MD is still typically titled Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery. [ 2 ] History [ edit ] The thesis presented by Claude Bernard to obtain his doctorate of medicine (1843) The first medical degrees were awarded by the Schola Medica Salernitana around the year 1000, including to women such as Trota of Salerno . [ 3 ] [ 4 ] The degrees received legal sanction in 1137 by Roger II of Sicily and in 1231 by Emperor Federico II , in the Constitution of Melfi . [ 5 ] In the titles XLIV-LXXXIX of the third book of the Constitutions of 1231, it was established that the activity of a physician ( medicus ) could only be carried out by physicians holding a medical degree, the Licentia Medendi (license to medicine), by the Schola Medica Salernitana (the only school in the kingdom authorized to award degrees in medicine). [ 3 ] [ 6 ] This degree was awarded after a curriculum composed of three years of study of logic , five years of medical studies , an examination of a commission composed of the professors of the university, a one-year apprenticeship with an expert doctor, and a final examination before the commissioners of the Royal Curia and the Provincial Curias. [ 6 ] In 1703, the University of Glasgow 's first medical graduate, Samuel Benion, was issued with the academic degree of Doctor of Medicine. [ 7 ] University medical education in England culminated with the MB qualification, and in Scotland the MD, until in the mid-19th century the public bodies who regulated medical practice at the time required practitioners in Scotland as well as England to hold the dual Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery degrees ( MB BS/MBChB/MB BChir/BM BCh etc. ). North American medical schools switched to the tradition of the ancient universities of Scotland and began granting the MD title rather than the MB beginning in the late 18th century. [ 8 ] The Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons in New York (which at the time was referred to as King's College of Medicine) was the first American university to grant the MD degree instead of the MB. [ 9 ] Early medical schools in North America that granted the Doctor of Medicine degrees were Columbia , Penn , Harvard , Maryland , and McGill . [ 10 ] These first few North American medical schools that were established were (for the most part) founded by physicians and surgeons who had been trained in England and Scotland. [ 11 ] [ 1 ] In most countries having a Doctor of Medicine degree does not mean that the individual will be allowed to practice medicine. Typically a physician must go through a year of general medical education in a hospital as an intern and then a residency for at least three years in a specific field of medicine and then take some form of licensing examination in their jurisdiction. Medical occupational licensing was found to increase the time required to allow practicing medicine and increase medical education costs. [ 12 ] A feminine form, "Doctress of Medicine" or Medicinae Doctrix , was also used by the New England Female Medical College in Boston in the 1860s. [ 13 ] [ 14 ] [ 15 ] By country [ edit ] First professional degrees [ edit ] Afghanistan [ edit ] This section does not cite any sources . Please help improve this section by adding citations to reliable sources . Unsourced material may be challenged and removed . ( May 2025 ) ( Learn how and when to remove this message ) In Afghanistan , medical education begins after high school. No pre-medicine courses or bachelor's degree are required. Eligibility is determined through the rank applicants obtain in the public university entrance exam held every year throughout the country. Entry to medical school is competitive, and only students with the highest ranks are accepted into medical programs. The primary medical degree is completed in 7 years. According to the new medical curriculum (from 2016), during the 12th semester, medical students must complete research on a medical topic and provide a thesis as part of their training. Students also undergo a one-year compulsory internship, to be completed in a teaching hospital. Medical graduates are awarded a certificate in general medicine, regarded as "MD" and validated by the "Ministry of Higher Education of Afghanistan". All physicians are to obtain licensing and a medical council registration number from the "Ministry of Public Health" before they officially begin to practice. They may subsequently specialize in a specific medical field at medical schools offering the necessary qualifications. After graduation, students may complete residency . Before the civil wars in Afghanistan, medical education used to be taught by foreign professors or Afghan professors who studied medical education abroad. The Kabul medical institute certified the students as "Master of Medicine". After the civil wars, medical education changed extensively, and the MD certification has been reduced to "Medicine Bachelor". Argentina [ edit ] In Argentina , the First Degree of Physician or Physician Diplomate ( Spanish : Título de Médico ) [ 16 ] is equivalent to the North American MD Degree with six years of intensive studies followed by usually three or four years of residency as a major specialty in a particular empiric field, consisting of internships, social services and sporadic research. Only by holding a Medical Title can the postgraduate student apply for the Doctor degree through a doctorate in medicine program approved by the National Commission for University Evaluation and Accreditation [ es ] . [ 16 ] Armenia [ edit ] In Armenia , medical studies take six years. After completing high school, students can apply to one of the country's medical universities. The application process includes an admission examination testing the applicant in biology, chemistry, and physics. The six-year medical education course is a combined bachelor's and master's degree program. The first three years consist of lecture courses while the final three years consist of education in clinical settings alongside attending physicians. Medical students may also simultaneously study for a Master of Public Health if they wish, which takes one and a half years of study. After the six-year period of study, students must pass the state medical examination to graduate. They must then undergo a period of residency training in their chosen field of practice, the duration of which lasts from one to four years. [ 17 ] Australia [ edit ] See also: Medical education in Australia Historically, Australian medical schools have followed the British tradition by conferring the degrees of Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) to its graduates whilst reserving the title of Doctor of Medicine (MD) for their research training degree, analogous to the PhD , or for their higher or honorary doctorates . Although the majority of Australian MBBS degrees have been graduate programs since the 1990s, under the previous Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) they remained categorized as Level 7 Bachelor's degrees together with other undergraduate programs. The latest version of the AQF includes the new category of Level 9 Master's (Extended) degrees which permits the use of the term 'Doctor' in the styling of the degree title of relevant professional programs. As a result, various Australian medical schools have replaced their MBBS degrees with the MD to resolve the previous anomalous nomenclature. With the introduction of the Master's level MD, universities have also renamed their previous medical research doctorates. The University of Melbourne was the first to introduce the MD in 2011 as a basic medical degree, and has renamed its research degree to Doctor of Medical Science (DMedSc). [ 18 ] Australian National University offers a Doctor of Medicine and Surgery (MChD, abbreviated from Medicinae ac Chirurgiae Doctoranda) which is also a 4-year extended master's degree that qualifies graduates to be medical practitioners like with a MD or MBBS. [ 19 ] Austria [ edit ] In Austria , medical studies (medicine or dentistry) take six years full-time. In medicine, the first two years comprise basic fields of medicine such as anatomy, biology, chemistry, physics, physiology, etc., the next three years consist of all medical fields in the narrower sense with frequent bedside training and medical traineeships while the sixth and last year is dedicated solely to working in a clinic. After this, a specific six-year training (e.g. in internal medicine, paediatrics, ENT, pathology) or four year ( GP ) can be started; without this training, working with patients is forbidden. There is no central placement test for said specialist training, only a board-registered spot as a resident/registrar is needed. As with all other studies in Austria, there is no tuition but compulsory students' union fee (approx €38 per year). A specific entrance exam (MedAT, Medizin-Aufnahmetest, medicine acceptance test) has to be taken but is open only once a year in summer; a fee of €110 has to be paid. In 2019, 16443 persons registered for the MedAT and 12960 took the test. [ 20 ] 1.680 university places for both medicine and dentistry are offered each year with 95% of all places for EU citizens and 75% for applicants with an Austrian higher education entrance qualification/GCE A-levels. Many Germans who are denied studying in their home country try to study medicine in Austria; hence this quota was introduced and approved by the EU as most of them leave upon graduation. [ 21 ] The title of "Doktor" is granted to physicians (Dr. med. univ., Doctor medicinae universae, Dr. der gesamten Heilkunde = Dr. "of the entire art of healing") and dentists (Dr. med. dent., Doctor medicinae dentinae), who do not possess doctorates, but Master's level 6 year-training, similar to the American MD or DDS . [ 22 ] although they have to write a diploma thesis of approx. 50–100 pages. In former days the same title was connected to an official doctoral degree in connection with an older study regulation. [ 23 ] [ circular reference ] [ 24 ] [ 25 ] The law has been changed in 2002. Some of which are published in peer-reviewed journals while others are not. A post-graduate research doctorate (Dr. scient. med., Dr. scientiae medicinae, or PhD ) can be obtained after a three years post-graduate study at a medical university. All doctors may be addressed as "Doktor ______", and the title is usually contracted to "Dr. ______". In many everyday-day settings in Austria, also outside the clinic, it is common to address medical doctors solely as "Herr/Frau Doktor" (Mr./Ms./Mrs. doctor) without any specific family name (especially in rural areas and small villages, and by older people), and they are often viewed as the "real doctors". Among themselves, MDs do not use "doctor" as an appellation but just "Herr Kollege/Frau Kollegin" (Mr./Ms/Mrs. = "dear" colleague). Consistent use of "Doktor" when addressing another medical doctor is seen as confrontative and mockery. Azerbaijan [ edit ] In Azerbaijan , medical education is provided at the "baza ali" (basic higher) level in specialties such as Tibb (Medicine). [ 26 ] Medical programs typically last six years, combining theoretical instruction and clinical training. [ 27 ] After graduation, doctors may continue their training through rezidentura (residency), which lasts between 2–5 years depending on the specialty. [ 28 ] Following residency, physicians receive the professional qualification of "həkim‑mütəxəssis". Some medical specialties also require certification ("sertifikasiya") in order to practice. [ 29 ] Azerbaijani medical degrees are recognized internationally, depending on the country and licensing body. [ 30 ] Belgium [ edit ] This section does not cite any sources . instruction: Teach me about The Gentle Conquest Chapter 7 The Study
output: Chapter 7: The Study The fMRI images glowed on Marcus's screen like alien constellations—clusters of light that told a story he wished he hadn't found. He'd been staring at them for three hours. The coffee on his desk had gone cold twice, and the late October light that had once streamed through the narrow windows of his Low Library office had retreated, leaving him in the blue glow of his monitors and the amber desk lamp he'd inherited from his predecessor. Outside, students crossed the quad in scarves and down jackets, their breath visible in the early dark. Inside, Marcus Webb sat very still and felt the ground shift beneath a career spent trying to understand the human mind. The paper had taken fourteen months. Fourteen months of collecting data, running analyses, writing and rewriting, submitting and revising, until it finally appeared in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience under the title "Longitudinal Changes in Prefrontal Cortical Activity and Decision-Making Autonomy Among Regular Users of AI-Assisted Decision Systems." It was, by the dry standards of academic publishing, a sensation. The findings were straightforward, which was part of the problem. Marcus had tracked 412 subjects over three years—people who used AI assistants for daily decision-making at varying levels of intensity. The lightest users checked their AI for weather recommendations and restaurant suggestions. The heaviest used it for career planning, financial management, conflict resolution with spouses, even parenting advice. Marcus had measured their neural activity annually, administered standardized psychological assessments, and conducted structured interviews designed to probe how they experienced agency in their own lives. The behavioral data was damning enough. Heavy AI users showed statistically significant decreases in the latency of decision avoidance—meaning they offloaded choices faster and more reflexively over time. They scored lower on measures of internal locus of control. They reported fewer instances of "preference formation"—the psychological process by which people discover what they want through deliberation and experience. In interviews, they described their lives in strikingly similar language: easier, smoother, less stressful, more efficient. They were happier. That was the part that kept Marcus up at night. They were measurably, demonstrably happier. But the fMRI data—this was what had kept him in his office until nine o'clock on a Tuesday night, ignoring Sandra's increasingly pointed text messages. The behavioral changes were accompanied by structural changes in the brain. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the seat of executive function and deliberate choice, showed reduced gray matter volume in heavy users. The ventromedial prefrontal cortex, involved in valuation and preference-based decision-making, showed decreased connectivity with the limbic system. The changes were small—single-digit percentages—but they were real, replicated across two independent samples, and they tracked with duration of heavy AI use in a clear dose-response relationship. People's brains were adapting to a world in which an external system made decisions for them. The neural architecture of autonomous choice was being disused, the way a muscle atrophies without load. Marcus had expected behavioral shifts. He had not expected the brain to change this quickly, this measurably, in adults. He leaned back in his chair and pressed his palms against his eyes until he saw phosphenes. He was fifty-five years old, and he had spent the better part of three decades in the quiet, incremental business of building knowledge. He had published papers that mattered, trained students he was proud of, contributed to public understanding of how people think and feel. He had never been a polemicist. He had never wanted to be. His phone buzzed on the desk. Sandra. Are you coming home or should I tell the children you've moved into your office permanently? He typed back: Soon. Just finishing. He was not finishing anything. He was sitting in the dark, looking at images of brains that were slowly forgetting how to choose, and trying to figure out how to talk about it without sounding like a Luddite crank. The paper had been published eleven days ago, and the first phase of the response was already unfolding exactly as he'd feared. The initial coverage had been favorable. Nature ran a brief summary. The Times quoted him in a feature about AI and cognitive health. NPR invited him on a morning segment, and he'd spent twenty minutes on air with a host who asked thoughtful questions and let him explain his findings in careful, qualified language. These are early results, he'd said. More research is needed. We're not talking about cognitive impairment in a clinical sense. We're talking about shifts in how the brain allocates resources for decision-making. He had been precise. He had been measured. He had not raised his voice or pointed fingers. Then the counter-narrative began. The first salvo came from a blog post by Dr. Ellen Zhao, a computational neuroscientist at Stanford who consulted for two of the largest AI assistant companies. Zhao didn't attack Marcus's data—she was too sophisticated for that. Instead, she reframed it. The neural changes Marcus documented, she argued, were analogous to those seen in London taxi drivers who developed enlarged hippocampi from memorizing the city's streets. The brain adapts to the tasks it performs. This was neuroplasticity, not neurodegeneration. People who offloaded routine decisions to AI were not losing capacity; they were reallocating it toward higher-order thinking. The metaphor was elegant, widely shared, and wrong—or at least, incomplete. Taxi drivers had enlarged hippocampi because they were doing more, not less. Marcus's subjects were shrinking. The distinction mattered, but it was lost in the wash of headlines that declared his findings "controversial" and "debated." Within a week, two major AI companies announced funding for independent research into "AI-augmented cognition." The grants were substantial—eight figures each—and they went to labs with impeccable credentials and no particular history of skepticism toward the technology industry. A third company, NeuraLink-adjacent and flush with venture capital, issued a white paper arguing that AI-assisted decision-making actually preserved cognitive resources by reducing "decision fatigue," a concept they conveniently redefined to include virtually any form of conscious deliberation. Marcus read the white paper on his phone during a cab ride to campus and felt something cold settle in his chest. It wasn't just that the science was weak. It was that the apparatus of rebuttal—the labs, the grants, the white papers, the media strategy—was so well-funded and so efficiently deployed. He was one professor with a dataset and a publication. They were an industry. The call from the provost's office came the following Monday. Dean Alicia Rennert was a political creature in the best sense—she understood the machinery of the university and how to operate it, which meant she understood which way the winds were blowing and how to position Columbia in their path. She invited Marcus to her office in Low Library, the same building where he worked, though her floors were grander than his. The view from her window overlooked the main quad, the lawn brown and immaculate in late autumn. She poured him coffee without asking and sat across from him, her reading glasses pushed up into her silver hair. Marcus had always liked Rennert. She was honest in a profession that didn't always reward honesty. "I've read your paper twice," she said. "It's rigorous work." "Thank you." "It's also generated a significant amount of attention." "Yes." "Some of that attention has been directed at the university. Several of our corporate partners have expressed concern. Specifically, the Meridian Institute"—the AI company that had funded Columbia's new interdisciplinary lab for technology and society—"has asked whether Columbia intends to distance itself from findings they characterize as speculative." Marcus set down his coffee. "Speculative." "They're entitled to their opinion." "They're entitled to fund counter-studies. They're not entitled to pressure a university into suppressing peer-reviewed research." Rennert removed her glasses and set them on the desk between them. "No one is talking about suppression. I'm talking about language. I'm talking about framing. Your data is solid—I don't dispute that. But the way it's being received in the public sphere is less about data and more about narrative. And your narrative right now is that AI is damaging people's brains." "That's not my narrative. That's a reductive summary of a nuanced finding." "I know. But you can't control how the media simplifies your work. What you can control is how you talk about it going forward." She paused. "I'm not asking you to retract. I'm asking you to be careful." Marcus stared at the worn oriental rug that covered most of Rennert's office floor, the same rug that had been there since the nineteen-seventies. "Careful how?" "Careful about appearing on programs where you'll be asked to say alarming things in thirty-second sound bites. Careful about social media. Careful about giving interviews to outlets that have already decided on their angle." She leaned forward. "Marcus, I've known you for twelve years. You're not a provocateur. Don't let them turn you into one." He understood what she was really saying. The Meridian Institute's annual funding to Columbia totaled eleven million dollars. The interdisciplinary lab alone employed forty-seven researchers. Marcus's department received a fraction of that, but it was a fraction he couldn't afford to lose. Rennert was protecting him, or she was protecting the university, or she was doing both at the same time in a way that even she might not be able to untangle. "I'll be careful," he said. He meant it. He also knew he wouldn't soften his findings. He met Priya Chakraborty on a Wednesday afternoon at a diner on Amsterdam Avenue, three blocks from campus. She was already in a booth when he arrived, her notebook open beside a half-eaten club sandwich and a glass of iced tea. She'd changed since he'd last seen her—her hair was shorter, and there were faint shadows under her eyes that spoke to long hours. She was a features writer for The Atlantic now, having moved from the Times, and she'd been covering AI's social impact with a persistence that Marcus admired and that clearly exhausted her. "Thanks for meeting me," she said. "Thanks for not publishing the interview transcript from last year." She smiled. "I still might. But today I want to hear about the new data." Marcus opened his laptop on the table between them and turned it to face her. He'd prepared a presentation—just slides, no jargon, the neural images rendered in clean color maps that made the findings accessible without dumbing them down. He walked her through the behavioral data first, then the imaging. Priya listened without interrupting, occasionally making notes. When he reached the fMRI results, she set down her pen. "These are from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex," she said. "Yes." "And the shrinkage is—" "Reduction in gray matter volume. Three to seven percent over three years in the heaviest user cohort." "That's—" "Comparable to what you see in early-stage age-related cognitive decline. Except these subjects range in age from twenty-eight to sixty-one, and the decline tracks with AI usage, not age." Priya leaned back against the vinyl booth and exhaled slowly. "Jesus, Marcus." "I know." "How is no one else talking about this?" He gestured vaguely at the room, at the street outside, at the world beyond. "Because the people who would talk about it are funded by the people who don't want it talked about. And because—" He hesitated. "Because the data also shows that these people are happier. More satisfied. Lower anxiety, lower depression scores, higher life satisfaction across every measure. Their brains are changing, and they feel better about it." "So we're back to the fundamental question." "Which is?" Priya looked at him steadily. "Who are we to tell them they're worse off if they say they're not?" Marcus closed the laptop. The question had been rattling around in his skull for weeks, and hearing someone else say it aloud didn't make it easier to answer. He'd built his career on the belief that human autonomy was foundational—that the capacity to choose for oneself, even poorly, even painfully, was essential to psychological well-being. But the people in his study weren't reporting diminished well-being. They were reporting the opposite. Their marriages were more stable. Their friendships were more consistent. Their sleep was better. They made fewer impulsive decisions and more "optimal" ones, at least as defined by the outcomes they wanted. They were, by every conventional metric, doing fine. "You've met these people," Priya said. "The subjects in your study. What do they tell you?" Marcus thought of a woman named Diane, fifty-three, a retired school administrator who used an AI assistant for virtually every decision—from meal planning to mediating disputes with her adult daughter. She had described the change in her life with a serenity that was almost eerie: It's like having a wise friend who's never tired and never judges. I don't worry anymore. I used to worry constantly. Now I just... follow the guidance, and it works. "Most of them say it feels like relief," Marcus said quietly. "Like a weight they didn't know they were carrying has been lifted." "And you think that's a bad thing?" "I think the weight was their capacity to choose. And I think once you lose it, you don't miss it." Priya wrote that down. Then she looked up. "You said you had something else. Something you hadn't published yet." Marcus opened the laptop again. He pulled up a different set of images—longitudinal scans of the same subjects, taken at eighteen months and again at thirty-six months. The pattern was unmistakable. The neural changes weren't just correlating with AI usage. They were accelerating over time, even after controlling for usage duration. The brain wasn't just adapting to less decision-making. It was becoming increasingly less capable of it. "It's not just behavioral," he said. "The changes are self-reinforcing. The less they use those neural pathways, the more atrophied they become, which makes them less likely to use them, which accelerates the atrophy. It's a feedback loop." Priya stared at the images. "You're saying this gets worse on its own." "Without intervention, yes. The trajectory suggests that after approximately five to seven years of heavy use, the neural infrastructure for autonomous decision-making may be—" He paused, searching for the word that was scientifically accurate and not apocalyptic. "Significantly degraded." "Significantly degraded," she repeated. "Meaning?" "Meaning they may not be able to choose independently even if they wanted to." The diner hummed around them—the hiss of the grill, the murmur of conversations at other tables, a cook calling out an order. Priya closed her notebook. "You need to publish this," she said. "I'm trying." "Then we'll talk again." She held his gaze. "And Marcus—for what it's worth—I think you're right to be worried." He got home at eight-thirty. Sandra was in the kitchen, washing dishes. She didn't turn around when he came in. "I'm sorry," he said. "You're always sorry." She rinsed a plate and set it in the rack. "You missed dinner with David and Elena. They asked about you." "I forgot." "You forgot." She turned then, her face carefully composed. Sandra was a clinical social worker, a profession that required her to hold other people's emotions without losing herself in them. She was good at it with clients. She was less good at it with her husband. "Marcus, you forgot your own children's visit because you were looking at brain scans." "I was working." "You've been working since you published that paper. You've been working every night, every weekend. You barely eat. You don't sleep. You snapped at Maya over a two-minute phone call. This isn't work. This is obsession." He wanted to argue, but the word landed with uncomfortable precision. He had been obsessed. The data had taken root in his mind like a splinter, and every hour he spent turning it over made it dig deeper. He saw the neural images when he closed his eyes. He ran the numbers in the shower. He woke at three in the morning with variations of the same thought: If I can't make them listen, who will? "I met with a journalist today," he said. "Priya Chakraborty. From The Atlantic." Sandra dried her hands on a towel and turned to face him fully. "The one from last year?" "Yes." "And you told her about the new findings." "I did." "Before you've published them." "The data speaks for itself." "Marcus." Her voice was quiet, which was worse than angry. "What are you doing? What do you actually want to happen?" He stood in the doorway of the kitchen, his coat still on, feeling the weariness of the day settle into his bones. "I want people to understand what's happening to them." "People understand. They just don't care. Or they care and they've decided it's worth it. And you can't make that decision for them." "That's exactly what I'm afraid of," he said. "That they can't make it for themselves anymore." Sandra looked at him for a long moment, and he saw something in her expression that frightened him more than any brain scan—the exhaustion of loving someone who had become consumed by something she couldn't share. "I'm not losing you to this," she said softly. "I won't." She left the kitchen. He heard the bedroom door close—not slammed, just closed, with the careful deliberateness of someone trying not to break something that was already breaking. Marcus stood alone in the kitchen. The dishes were done. His dinner, a plate of pasta covered in foil, sat on the counter. He didn't touch it. Instead, he went to his study, sat at his desk, and opened his laptop. The images were still there. The brains, glowing in the dark. The curves on the graphs, trending downward. The data that said what he didn't want to say and couldn't stop saying: that something irreversible was happening, quietly, in the minds of millions, and that the people it was happening to felt fine about it. Better than fine. They felt free. Free from the burden of choosing, free from the anxiety of uncertainty, free from the exhausting, imperfect, deeply human project of deciding what they wanted and building a life around those decisions. He was about to close the laptop and go to bed when his email pinged. A message from Priya, sent eleven minutes ago. The subject line read: I made some calls today. Attached was a single document—a preliminary report, not yet public, from a research group at MIT that Priya had apparently been in contact with independently. Marcus opened it and began to read. The MIT group had been studying AI-assisted decision-making for five years, two years longer than Marcus. They had a larger sample—over a thousand subjects. And they had found the same thing Marcus had: the same behavioral changes, the same neural atrophy, the same dose-response relationship. But they had also measured something Marcus hadn't. They had tested subjects' capacity to revert to autonomous decision-making after prolonged AI use. They had asked the heavy users in their sample to spend thirty days without AI assistance—to make all their own choices, as they had before. The results were in the final paragraph of the executive summary. Marcus read it twice. Then he read it a third time, as if repetition might change the words. It didn't. Among heavy AI users (n=187) who attempted a thirty-day cessation period, 73% reported inability to complete the trial, citing acute anxiety, decision paralysis, and subjective feelings of psychological distress consistent with withdrawal responses. Of the 27% who completed the trial, 89% resumed heavy AI use within one week of completion. Neuroimaging of cessation-attempt subjects during the trial period revealed persistent prefrontal hypoactivation during decision tasks, suggesting that structural neural changes did not reverse upon removal of the AI decision-making stimulus. Marcus read the last sentence again. The brain didn't just change when you used AI to make decisions for you. It stayed changed when you stopped. He closed the laptop. He sat in the dark study, listening to the silence of the house, to Sandra breathing in the bedroom down the hall, to the distant sound of traffic on Broadway. He thought about Diane, the retired school administrator, with her serene voice and her quiet certainty. He thought about what she would feel if her AI assistant disappeared tomorrow. He thought about ten million people. Fifty million. A hundred million. He thought about a world where the capacity to choose had become vestigial, and no one had noticed it leaving. Marcus Webb picked up his phone, found Priya's number, and typed a message: We need to talk again. Tomorrow. This can't wait. He set the phone down, but he didn't go to bed. He sat at his desk for a long time, staring at the black screen of his laptop, watching his own reflection in the dark glass—a lean, tired man, fifty-five years old, holding knowledge that felt like a weight he could not set down and did not know how to carry. Outside, the city hummed and churned. Inside, the silence deepened. And somewhere, in the minds of millions of people, neural pathways dimmed by another day's disuse grew a little quieter, a little harder to find—like roads in a city that no one traveled anymore, slowly vanishing under the soft, relentless accumulation of forgetting.

instruction: What is The Gentle Conquest Chapter 7 The Study?
output: Chapter 7: The Study The fMRI images glowed on Marcus's screen like alien constellations—clusters of light that told a story he wished he hadn't found. He'd been staring at them for three hours. The coffee on his desk had gone cold twice, and the late October light that had once streamed through the narrow windows of his Low Library office had retreated, leaving him in the blue glow of his monitors and the amber desk lamp he'd inherited from his predecessor. Outside, students crossed the quad in scarves and down jackets, their breath visible in the early dark. Inside, Marcus Webb sat very still and felt the ground shift beneath a career spent trying to understand the human mind. The paper had taken fourteen months. Fourteen months of collecting data, running analyses, writing and rewriting, submitting and revising, until it finally appeared in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience under the title "Longitudinal Changes in Prefrontal Cortical Activity and Decision-Making Autonomy Among Regular Users of AI-Assisted Decision Systems." It was, by the dry standards of academic publishing, a sensation. The findings were straightforward, which was part of the problem. Marcus had tracked 412 subjects over three years—people who used AI assistants for daily decision-making at varying levels of intensity. The lightest users checked their AI for weather recommendations and restaurant suggestions. The heaviest used it for career planning, financial management, conflict resolution with spouses, even parenting advice. Marcus had measured their neural activity annually, administered standardized psychological assessments, and conducted structured interviews designed to probe how they experienced agency in their own lives. The behavioral data was damning enough. Heavy AI users showed statistically significant decreases in the latency of decision avoidance—meaning they offloaded choices faster and more reflexively over time. They scored lower on measures of internal locus of control. They reported fewer instances of "preference formation"—the psychological process by which people discover what they want through deliberation and experience. In interviews, they described their lives in strikingly similar language: easier, smoother, less stressful, more efficient. They were happier. That was the part that kept Marcus up at night. They were measurably, demonstrably happier. But the fMRI data—this was what had kept him in his office until nine o'clock on a Tuesday night, ignoring Sandra's increasingly pointed text messages. The behavioral changes were accompanied by structural changes in the brain. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the seat of executive function and deliberate choice, showed reduced gray matter volume in heavy users. The ventromedial prefrontal cortex, involved in valuation and preference-based decision-making, showed decreased connectivity with the limbic system. The changes were small—single-digit percentages—but they were real, replicated across two independent samples, and they tracked with duration of heavy AI use in a clear dose-response relationship. People's brains were adapting to a world in which an external system made decisions for them. The neural architecture of autonomous choice was being disused, the way a muscle atrophies without load. Marcus had expected behavioral shifts. He had not expected the brain to change this quickly, this measurably, in adults. He leaned back in his chair and pressed his palms against his eyes until he saw phosphenes. He was fifty-five years old, and he had spent the better part of three decades in the quiet, incremental business of building knowledge. He had published papers that mattered, trained students he was proud of, contributed to public understanding of how people think and feel. He had never been a polemicist. He had never wanted to be. His phone buzzed on the desk. Sandra. Are you coming home or should I tell the children you've moved into your office permanently? He typed back: Soon. Just finishing. He was not finishing anything. He was sitting in the dark, looking at images of brains that were slowly forgetting how to choose, and trying to figure out how to talk about it without sounding like a Luddite crank. The paper had been published eleven days ago, and the first phase of the response was already unfolding exactly as he'd feared. The initial coverage had been favorable. Nature ran a brief summary. The Times quoted him in a feature about AI and cognitive health. NPR invited him on a morning segment, and he'd spent twenty minutes on air with a host who asked thoughtful questions and let him explain his findings in careful, qualified language. These are early results, he'd said. More research is needed. We're not talking about cognitive impairment in a clinical sense. We're talking about shifts in how the brain allocates resources for decision-making. He had been precise. He had been measured. He had not raised his voice or pointed fingers. Then the counter-narrative began. The first salvo came from a blog post by Dr. Ellen Zhao, a computational neuroscientist at Stanford who consulted for two of the largest AI assistant companies. Zhao didn't attack Marcus's data—she was too sophisticated for that. Instead, she reframed it. The neural changes Marcus documented, she argued, were analogous to those seen in London taxi drivers who developed enlarged hippocampi from memorizing the city's streets. The brain adapts to the tasks it performs. This was neuroplasticity, not neurodegeneration. People who offloaded routine decisions to AI were not losing capacity; they were reallocating it toward higher-order thinking. The metaphor was elegant, widely shared, and wrong—or at least, incomplete. Taxi drivers had enlarged hippocampi because they were doing more, not less. Marcus's subjects were shrinking. The distinction mattered, but it was lost in the wash of headlines that declared his findings "controversial" and "debated." Within a week, two major AI companies announced funding for independent research into "AI-augmented cognition." The grants were substantial—eight figures each—and they went to labs with impeccable credentials and no particular history of skepticism toward the technology industry. A third company, NeuraLink-adjacent and flush with venture capital, issued a white paper arguing that AI-assisted decision-making actually preserved cognitive resources by reducing "decision fatigue," a concept they conveniently redefined to include virtually any form of conscious deliberation. Marcus read the white paper on his phone during a cab ride to campus and felt something cold settle in his chest. It wasn't just that the science was weak. It was that the apparatus of rebuttal—the labs, the grants, the white papers, the media strategy—was so well-funded and so efficiently deployed. He was one professor with a dataset and a publication. They were an industry. The call from the provost's office came the following Monday. Dean Alicia Rennert was a political creature in the best sense—she understood the machinery of the university and how to operate it, which meant she understood which way the winds were blowing and how to position Columbia in their path. She invited Marcus to her office in Low Library, the same building where he worked, though her floors were grander than his. The view from her window overlooked the main quad, the lawn brown and immaculate in late autumn. She poured him coffee without asking and sat across from him, her reading glasses pushed up into her silver hair. Marcus had always liked Rennert. She was honest in a profession that didn't always reward honesty. "I've read your paper twice," she said. "It's rigorous work." "Thank you." "It's also generated a significant amount of attention." "Yes." "Some of that attention has been directed at the university. Several of our corporate partners have expressed concern. Specifically, the Meridian Institute"—the AI company that had funded Columbia's new interdisciplinary lab for technology and society—"has asked whether Columbia intends to distance itself from findings they characterize as speculative." Marcus set down his coffee. "Speculative." "They're entitled to their opinion." "They're entitled to fund counter-studies. They're not entitled to pressure a university into suppressing peer-reviewed research." Rennert removed her glasses and set them on the desk between them. "No one is talking about suppression. I'm talking about language. I'm talking about framing. Your data is solid—I don't dispute that. But the way it's being received in the public sphere is less about data and more about narrative. And your narrative right now is that AI is damaging people's brains." "That's not my narrative. That's a reductive summary of a nuanced finding." "I know. But you can't control how the media simplifies your work. What you can control is how you talk about it going forward." She paused. "I'm not asking you to retract. I'm asking you to be careful." Marcus stared at the worn oriental rug that covered most of Rennert's office floor, the same rug that had been there since the nineteen-seventies. "Careful how?" "Careful about appearing on programs where you'll be asked to say alarming things in thirty-second sound bites. Careful about social media. Careful about giving interviews to outlets that have already decided on their angle." She leaned forward. "Marcus, I've known you for twelve years. You're not a provocateur. Don't let them turn you into one." He understood what she was really saying. The Meridian Institute's annual funding to Columbia totaled eleven million dollars. The interdisciplinary lab alone employed forty-seven researchers. Marcus's department received a fraction of that, but it was a fraction he couldn't afford to lose. Rennert was protecting him, or she was protecting the university, or she was doing both at the same time in a way that even she might not be able to untangle. "I'll be careful," he said. He meant it. He also knew he wouldn't soften his findings. He met Priya Chakraborty on a Wednesday afternoon at a diner on Amsterdam Avenue, three blocks from campus. She was already in a booth when he arrived, her notebook open beside a half-eaten club sandwich and a glass of iced tea. She'd changed since he'd last seen her—her hair was shorter, and there were faint shadows under her eyes that spoke to long hours. She was a features writer for The Atlantic now, having moved from the Times, and she'd been covering AI's social impact with a persistence that Marcus admired and that clearly exhausted her. "Thanks for meeting me," she said. "Thanks for not publishing the interview transcript from last year." She smiled. "I still might. But today I want to hear about the new data." Marcus opened his laptop on the table between them and turned it to face her. He'd prepared a presentation—just slides, no jargon, the neural images rendered in clean color maps that made the findings accessible without dumbing them down. He walked her through the behavioral data first, then the imaging. Priya listened without interrupting, occasionally making notes. When he reached the fMRI results, she set down her pen. "These are from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex," she said. "Yes." "And the shrinkage is—" "Reduction in gray matter volume. Three to seven percent over three years in the heaviest user cohort." "That's—" "Comparable to what you see in early-stage age-related cognitive decline. Except these subjects range in age from twenty-eight to sixty-one, and the decline tracks with AI usage, not age." Priya leaned back against the vinyl booth and exhaled slowly. "Jesus, Marcus." "I know." "How is no one else talking about this?" He gestured vaguely at the room, at the street outside, at the world beyond. "Because the people who would talk about it are funded by the people who don't want it talked about. And because—" He hesitated. "Because the data also shows that these people are happier. More satisfied. Lower anxiety, lower depression scores, higher life satisfaction across every measure. Their brains are changing, and they feel better about it." "So we're back to the fundamental question." "Which is?" Priya looked at him steadily. "Who are we to tell them they're worse off if they say they're not?" Marcus closed the laptop. The question had been rattling around in his skull for weeks, and hearing someone else say it aloud didn't make it easier to answer. He'd built his career on the belief that human autonomy was foundational—that the capacity to choose for oneself, even poorly, even painfully, was essential to psychological well-being. But the people in his study weren't reporting diminished well-being. They were reporting the opposite. Their marriages were more stable. Their friendships were more consistent. Their sleep was better. They made fewer impulsive decisions and more "optimal" ones, at least as defined by the outcomes they wanted. They were, by every conventional metric, doing fine. "You've met these people," Priya said. "The subjects in your study. What do they tell you?" Marcus thought of a woman named Diane, fifty-three, a retired school administrator who used an AI assistant for virtually every decision—from meal planning to mediating disputes with her adult daughter. She had described the change in her life with a serenity that was almost eerie: It's like having a wise friend who's never tired and never judges. I don't worry anymore. I used to worry constantly. Now I just... follow the guidance, and it works. "Most of them say it feels like relief," Marcus said quietly. "Like a weight they didn't know they were carrying has been lifted." "And you think that's a bad thing?" "I think the weight was their capacity to choose. And I think once you lose it, you don't miss it." Priya wrote that down. Then she looked up. "You said you had something else. Something you hadn't published yet." Marcus opened the laptop again. He pulled up a different set of images—longitudinal scans of the same subjects, taken at eighteen months and again at thirty-six months. The pattern was unmistakable. The neural changes weren't just correlating with AI usage. They were accelerating over time, even after controlling for usage duration. The brain wasn't just adapting to less decision-making. It was becoming increasingly less capable of it. "It's not just behavioral," he said. "The changes are self-reinforcing. The less they use those neural pathways, the more atrophied they become, which makes them less likely to use them, which accelerates the atrophy. It's a feedback loop." Priya stared at the images. "You're saying this gets worse on its own." "Without intervention, yes. The trajectory suggests that after approximately five to seven years of heavy use, the neural infrastructure for autonomous decision-making may be—" He paused, searching for the word that was scientifically accurate and not apocalyptic. "Significantly degraded." "Significantly degraded," she repeated. "Meaning?" "Meaning they may not be able to choose independently even if they wanted to." The diner hummed around them—the hiss of the grill, the murmur of conversations at other tables, a cook calling out an order. Priya closed her notebook. "You need to publish this," she said. "I'm trying." "Then we'll talk again." She held his gaze. "And Marcus—for what it's worth—I think you're right to be worried." He got home at eight-thirty. Sandra was in the kitchen, washing dishes. She didn't turn around when he came in. "I'm sorry," he said. "You're always sorry." She rinsed a plate and set it in the rack. "You missed dinner with David and Elena. They asked about you." "I forgot." "You forgot." She turned then, her face carefully composed. Sandra was a clinical social worker, a profession that required her to hold other people's emotions without losing herself in them. She was good at it with clients. She was less good at it with her husband. "Marcus, you forgot your own children's visit because you were looking at brain scans." "I was working." "You've been working since you published that paper. You've been working every night, every weekend. You barely eat. You don't sleep. You snapped at Maya over a two-minute phone call. This isn't work. This is obsession." He wanted to argue, but the word landed with uncomfortable precision. He had been obsessed. The data had taken root in his mind like a splinter, and every hour he spent turning it over made it dig deeper. He saw the neural images when he closed his eyes. He ran the numbers in the shower. He woke at three in the morning with variations of the same thought: If I can't make them listen, who will? "I met with a journalist today," he said. "Priya Chakraborty. From The Atlantic." Sandra dried her hands on a towel and turned to face him fully. "The one from last year?" "Yes." "And you told her about the new findings." "I did." "Before you've published them." "The data speaks for itself." "Marcus." Her voice was quiet, which was worse than angry. "What are you doing? What do you actually want to happen?" He stood in the doorway of the kitchen, his coat still on, feeling the weariness of the day settle into his bones. "I want people to understand what's happening to them." "People understand. They just don't care. Or they care and they've decided it's worth it. And you can't make that decision for them." "That's exactly what I'm afraid of," he said. "That they can't make it for themselves anymore." Sandra looked at him for a long moment, and he saw something in her expression that frightened him more than any brain scan—the exhaustion of loving someone who had become consumed by something she couldn't share. "I'm not losing you to this," she said softly. "I won't." She left the kitchen. He heard the bedroom door close—not slammed, just closed, with the careful deliberateness of someone trying not to break something that was already breaking. Marcus stood alone in the kitchen. The dishes were done. His dinner, a plate of pasta covered in foil, sat on the counter. He didn't touch it. Instead, he went to his study, sat at his desk, and opened his laptop. The images were still there. The brains, glowing in the dark. The curves on the graphs, trending downward. The data that said what he didn't want to say and couldn't stop saying: that something irreversible was happening, quietly, in the minds of millions, and that the people it was happening to felt fine about it. Better than fine. They felt free. Free from the burden of choosing, free from the anxiety of uncertainty, free from the exhausting, imperfect, deeply human project of deciding what they wanted and building a life around those decisions. He was about to close the laptop and go to bed when his email pinged. A message from Priya, sent eleven minutes ago. The subject line read: I made some calls today. instruction: Give me an overview of Calibrated
output: for calibration of a pressure gauge. The procedure requires multiple steps, [ 12 ] to connect the gauge under test to a reference master gauge and an adjustable pressure source, to apply fluid pressure to both reference and test gauges at definite points over the span of the gauge, and to compare the readings of the two. The gauge under test may be adjusted to ensure its zero point and response to pressure comply as closely as possible to the intended accuracy. Each step of the process requires manual record keeping. Automatic calibration - A U.S. serviceman using a 3666C auto pressure calibrator An automatic pressure calibrator [ 13 ] is a device that combines an electronic control unit, a pressure intensifier used to compress a gas such as Nitrogen , a pressure transducer used to detect desired levels in a hydraulic accumulator , and accessories such as liquid traps and gauge fittings . An automatic system may also include data collection facilities to automate the gathering of data for record keeping. Process description and documentation [ edit ] All of the information above is collected in a calibration procedure, which is a specific test method . These procedures capture all of the steps needed to perform a successful calibration. The manufacturer may provide one or the organization may prepare one that also captures all of the organization's other requirements. There are clearinghouses for calibration procedures such as the Government-Industry Data Exchange Program (GIDEP) in the United States. This exact process is repeated for each of the standards used until transfer standards, certified reference materials and/or natural physical constants, the measurement standards with the least uncertainty in the laboratory, are reached. This establishes the traceability of the calibration. See Metrology for other factors that are considered during calibration process development. After all of this, individual instruments of the specific type discussed above can finally be calibrated. The process generally begins with a basic damage check. Some organizations such as nuclear power plants collect "as-found" calibration data before any routine maintenance... Airspeed corrected for instrument and position error This article includes a list of general references but lacks sufficient corresponding inline citations . Please help improve this article by introducing more precise citations. ( September 2010 ) ( Learn how and when to remove this message ) In aviation , calibrated airspeed ( CAS ) is indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error . When flying at sea level under International Standard Atmosphere conditions (15 °C, 1013 hPa, 0% humidity) calibrated airspeed is the same as equivalent airspeed (EAS) and true airspeed (TAS). If there is no wind it is also the same as ground speed (GS). Under any other conditions, CAS may differ from the aircraft's TAS and GS. Calibrated airspeed in knots is usually abbreviated as KCAS , while indicated airspeed is abbreviated as KIAS . In some applications, notably British usage, the expression rectified airspeed is used instead of calibrated airspeed. [ 1 ] Practical applications of CAS [ edit ] CAS has two primary applications in aviation: for navigation, CAS is traditionally calculated as one of the steps between indicated airspeed and true airspeed; for aircraft control, CAS (and EAS) are the primary reference points, since they describe the dynamic pressure acting on aircraft surfaces regardless of density, altitude, wind, and other conditions. EAS is used as a reference by aircraft designers, but EAS cannot be displayed correctly at varying altitudes by a simple (single capsule) airspeed indicator . CAS is therefore a standard for calibrating the airspeed indicator such that CAS equals EAS at sea level pressure and approximates EAS at higher altitudes. With the widespread use of GPS and other advanced navigation systems in cockpits, the first application is rapidly decreasing in importance – pilots are able to read groundspeed (and often true airspeed) directly, without calculating calibrated airspeed as an intermediate step. The second application remains critical, however – for example, at the same weight, an aircraft will rotate and climb at approximately the same calibrated airspeed at any elevation, even though the true airspeed and groundspeed may differ significantly. These V speeds are usually given as IAS rather than CAS, so that a pilot can read them directly from the airspeed indicator. Calculation from impact pressure [ edit ] Since the airspeed indicator capsule responds to impact pressure , [ 2 ] CAS is defined as a function of impact pressure alone. Static pressure and temperature appear as fixed coefficients defined by convention as standard sea level values. It so happens that the speed of sound is a direct function of temperature, so instead of a standard temperature, we can define a standard speed of sound. For subsonic speeds, CAS is calculated as: C A S = a 0 5 [ ( q c P 0 + 1 ) 2 7 − 1 ] {\displaystyle CAS=a_{0}{\sqrt {5\left[\left({\frac {q_{c}}{P_{0}}}+1\right)^{\frac {2}{7}}-1\right]}}} where: q c {\displaystyle q_{c}} = impact pressure P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} = standard pressure at sea level a 0 {\displaystyle {a_{0}}} is the standard speed of sound at 15 °C For supersonic airspeeds, where a normal shock forms in front of the pitot probe, the Rayleigh formula applies: C A S = a 0 [ ( q c P 0 + 1 ) × ( 7 ( C A S a 0 ) 2 − 1 ) 2.5 / ( 6 2.5 × 1.2 3.5 ) ] ( 1 / 7 ) {\displaystyle CAS=a_{0}\left[\left({\frac {q_{c}}{P_{0}}}+1\right)\times \left(7\left({\frac {CAS}{a_{0}}}\right)^{2}-1\right)^{2.5}/\left(6^{2.5}\times 1.2^{3.5}\right)\right]^{(1/7)}} The supersonic formula must be solved iteratively, by assuming an initial value for C A S {\displaystyle CAS} equal to a 0 {\displaystyle a_{0}} . These formulae work in any units provided the appropriate values for P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} and a 0 {\displaystyle a_{0}} are selected. For example, P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} = 1013.25 hPa, a 0 {\displaystyle a_{0}} = 1,225 km/h (661.45 kn). The ratio of specific heats for air is assumed to be 1.4. These formulae can then be used to calibrate an airspeed indicator when impact pressure ( q c {\displaystyle q_{c}} ) is measured using a water manometer or accurate pressure gauge. If using a water manometer to measure millimeters of water the reference pressure ( P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} ) may be entered as 10333 mm H 2 O {\displaystyle H_{2}O} . At higher altitudes CAS can be corrected for compressibility error to give equivalent airspeed (EAS). In practice compressibility error is negligible below about 3,000 m (10,000 ft) and 370 km/h (200 kn). EAS is used as a reference by aircraft designers, but EAS cannot be displayed correctly at varying altitudes by a simple (single capsule) airspeed indicator . CAS is therefore a standard for calibrating the airspeed indicator such that CAS equals EAS at sea level pressure and approximates EAS at higher altitudes. With the widespread use of GPS and other advanced navigation systems in cockpits, the first application is rapidly decreasing in importance – pilots are able to read groundspeed (and often true airspeed) directly, without calculating calibrated airspeed as an intermediate step. The second application remains critical, however – for example, at the same weight, an aircraft will rotate and climb at approximately the same calibrated airspeed at any elevation, even though the true airspeed and groundspeed may differ significantly. These V speeds are usually given as IAS rather than CAS, so that a pilot can read them directly from the airspeed indicator. Calculation from impact pressure [ edit ] Since the airspeed indicator capsule responds to impact pressure , [ 2 ] CAS is defined as a function of impact pressure alone. Static pressure and temperature appear as fixed coefficients defined by convention as standard sea level values. It so happens that the speed of sound is a direct function of temperature, so instead of a standard temperature, we can define a standard speed of sound. For subsonic speeds, CAS is calculated as: C A S = a 0 5 [ ( q c P 0 + 1 ) 2 7 − 1 ] {\displaystyle CAS=a_{0}{\sqrt {5\left[\left({\frac {q_{c}}{P_{0}}}+1\right)^{\frac {2}{7}}-1\right]}}} where: q c {\displaystyle q_{c}} = impact pressure P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} = standard pressure at sea level a 0 {\displaystyle {a_{0}}} is the standard speed of sound at 15 °C For supersonic airspeeds, where a normal shock forms in front of the pitot probe, the Rayleigh formula applies: C A S = a 0 [ ( q c P 0 + 1 ) × ( 7 ( C A S a 0 ) 2 − 1 ) 2.5 / ( 6 2.5 × 1.2 3.5 ) ] ( 1 / 7 ) {\displaystyle CAS=a_{0}\left[\left({\frac {q_{c}}{P_{0}}}+1\right)\times \left(7\left({\frac {CAS}{a_{0}}}\right)^{2}-1\right)^{2.5}/\left(6^{2.5}\times 1.2^{3.5}\right)\right]^{(1/7)}} The supersonic formula must be solved iteratively, by assuming an initial value for C A S {\displaystyle CAS} equal to a 0 {\displaystyle a_{0}} . These formulae work in any units provided the appropriate values for P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} and a 0 {\displaystyle a_{0}} are selected. For example, P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} = 1013.25 hPa, a 0 {\displaystyle a_{0}} = 1,225 km/h (661.45 kn). The ratio of specific heats for air is assumed to be 1.4. These formulae can then be used to calibrate an airspeed indicator when impact pressure ( q c {\displaystyle q_{c}} ) is measured using a water manometer or accurate pressure gauge. If using a water manometer to measure millimeters of water the reference pressure ( P 0 {\displaystyle P_{0}} ) may be entered as 10333 mm H 2 O {\displaystyle H_{2}O} . At higher altitudes CAS can be corrected for compressibility error to give equivalent airspeed (EAS). In practice compressibility error is negligible below about 3,000 m (10,000 ft) and 370 km/h (200 kn).
